stem: FISCAL POLICY refers to government use of:

options.option_text: Interest rates set by the central bank
Foreign exchange reserves only as tool
Currency devaluation as the chief policy

explanation: FISCAL policy = Government's use of TAXATION + SPENDING to influence economy. Set by Finance Ministry / Govt. Tools: tax rates, subsidy, public spending, borrowing. EXPANSIONARY (boost growth): cut taxes, raise spending → stimulates demand, but raises deficit. CONTRACTIONARY (curb inflation): raise taxes, cut spending. Distractor 1 = MONETARY policy (RBI). Distractor 4 = exchange rate policy. Both fiscal + monetary policies are macroeconomic levers; ideally coordinated.
subject: Economics

stem: FISCAL DEFICIT (FD) is defined as:

options.option_text: Revenue receipts minus revenue expenditure (revenue gap)
Total expenditure minus total receipts (excluding borrowing)
Capital receipts minus capital expenditure (capital gap)
Tax revenue minus subsidy spending of govt budget

explanation: FISCAL DEFICIT = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts (EXCLUDING BORROWINGS). i.e., the GAP that government fills by borrowing. India's FD target (FRBM) was 3% of GDP; suspended during pandemic; FY24 ~5.6%, glide path to 4.5% by FY26. Other deficits: REVENUE DEFICIT = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts (= 'living beyond means'); PRIMARY DEFICIT = FD − interest payments (true gap excluding past-debt servicing); EFFECTIVE REVENUE DEFICIT = RD − grants for capital creation. FD financed by: market borrowing (G-secs), small savings, foreign loans, RBI ways-and-means.
subject: Economics

stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT TAX in India?

options.option_text: Excise duty on alcohol or fuel

explanation: DIRECT TAX = paid DIRECTLY by the person on whom it's levied; cannot be shifted. Examples: INCOME TAX (individuals + companies), CORPORATE TAX, CAPITAL GAINS TAX. Govt body: CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes). INDIRECT TAX = levied on goods/services; can be shifted to consumers (built into price). Examples: GST (replaced excise, service tax, VAT, etc., from July 2017), CUSTOMS DUTY (on imports — and few exports), STAMP DUTY (state-level). Govt body: CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes + Customs). Indian taxes: ~50% direct + ~50% indirect (varies year to year).
subject: Economics

stem: FRBM Act (Fiscal Responsibility + Budget Management Act, 2003) was enacted to:

options.option_text: Increase government borrowing limits in budget
Increase tax rates substantially every year

explanation: FRBM ACT, 2003 — enacted to bring fiscal discipline. Targets: (1) eliminate revenue deficit by FY09 (postponed); (2) reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP. RBI ways-and-means lending to govt phased out by 2006. RBI cannot subscribe to PRIMARY auction of govt bonds (must buy in secondary market). Original targets often missed + RELAXED. Pandemic 2020 → suspended. Current glide path: FD to 4.5% of GDP by FY26 (FY24 actual ~5.6%). Critics argue FRBM is too rigid; defenders say discipline avoids crowding out + fiscal crisis. NK SINGH committee (2017) recommended 'debt rule' framework (debt-to-GDP target).
subject: Economics

stem: GST (Goods and Services Tax) rolled out in India on:
explanation: GST launched at MIDNIGHT 1 JULY 2017 — special joint session of Parliament. Replaced ~17 indirect taxes (excise, service tax, VAT, OCTROI, entertainment, luxury, central sales tax). 'ONE NATION, ONE TAX'. 4 main rate slabs: 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (+ 0% essentials, special 0.25% gold, special 3% gold). GST COUNCIL (chair: Finance Minister; 1 minister per state) decides rates. INPUT TAX CREDIT — businesses claim back tax paid on inputs. CGST + SGST + IGST (interstate). 101st Amendment Act (2016) enabled GST. Implementation initially rocky (multiple slabs, compliance burden) — gradually streamlined. Approved by every state + UT.
subject: Economics

stem: REVENUE RECEIPTS of the central government primarily come from:

options.option_text: Sale of public sector enterprises in budget
Borrowing from Reserve Bank of India only
Foreign aid + grants from foreign countries

explanation: REVENUE RECEIPTS = TAX REVENUE (income tax, GST, customs, corporation, excise) + NON-TAX REVENUE (interest on loans, dividends from PSUs, fees, fines, RBI surplus, spectrum auction in part). CAPITAL RECEIPTS = borrowing (mostly market loans), disinvestment (sale of stake in PSUs), recoveries of loans. NOT a 'receipt' but financing: RBI ways-and-means / OD. Distractor 1 = capital (disinvestment). Distractor 3 = capital. Distractor 4 = small fraction.
subject: Economics

stem: The annual UNION BUDGET in India is presented by:

options.option_text: Prime Minister of India in Parliament
Finance Minister of Govt of India
RBI Governor from the Mumbai office
Niti Aayog Chairman in the Parliament

explanation: UNION BUDGET = Annual Financial Statement (Article 112). Presented by FINANCE MINISTER in Lok Sabha, traditionally on the LAST WORKING DAY OF FEBRUARY at 5 PM, but from FY18 shifted to 1 FEBRUARY at 11 AM (allows Parliament to pass before April 1 fiscal year start). RAILWAY BUDGET (separate since 1924) merged with UNION BUDGET from 2017. Indira GANDHI (1969) — only PM to present budget (held FM portfolio briefly). MORARJI DESAI presented MOST budgets (10). NIRMALA SITHARAMAN (since 2019) — first full-time woman FM (Indira had been acting FM); has presented 6 budgets (FY 20-25). Special: 'KAR LAGE BAHI' (a tradition the PM once thanked her for, ditched in 2019).
subject: Economics

stem: The Union Budget in India is presented under which Article of the Constitution?
subject: Economics
explanation: Article 112 of the Indian Constitution provides for the Annual Financial Statement (the Union Budget).

stem: Which of the following is NOT an instrument of fiscal policy?
subject: Economics
explanation: Open market operations are an instrument of monetary policy (conducted by RBI). Fiscal policy tools include government spending, taxation, and public debt.

stem: Fiscal deficit is defined as:

options.option_text: Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings

subject: Economics
explanation: Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − Total receipts (excluding borrowings). It represents the government's borrowing requirement.

stem: Revenue deficit = ?
subject: Economics
explanation: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts. It shows the excess of day-to-day expenditure over income.

stem: Primary deficit = ?
subject: Economics
explanation: Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments. It shows the government's borrowing need excluding interest obligations.

stem: Expansionary fiscal policy involves:

options.option_text: Increasing government spending or reducing taxes to stimulate demand

subject: Economics
explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy stimulates aggregate demand through higher spending or lower taxes, typically used during recessions.

stem: The FRBM Act, 2003 stands for:

options.option_text: Financial Reforms and Budget Management Act
Federal Reserve and Banking Management Act
Foreign Revenue and Borrowing Management Act
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act

subject: Economics
explanation: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 was enacted to ensure fiscal discipline and reduce the fiscal deficit.

stem: Which of the following is a direct tax?
subject: Economics
explanation: Income Tax is a direct tax — levied on and paid directly by the person who earns the income. GST, excise, and customs are indirect taxes.

stem: Disinvestment by the government means:

options.option_text: Government selling its stake in public sector undertakings

subject: Economics
explanation: Disinvestment refers to the government selling a portion or all of its equity in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) to generate revenue.

stem: Which committee recommended the target of 3% fiscal deficit to GDP for the Centre?
subject: Economics
explanation: The N.K. Singh Committee (FRBM Review Committee, 2017) recommended the 3% fiscal deficit target and introducing a Fiscal Council.

stem: Which type of budget reflects income equality aims by taxing the rich more and spending on welfare?
subject: Economics
explanation: A progressive or welfare-oriented budget taxes higher incomes at higher rates and directs spending toward social welfare, reducing income inequality.

stem: The 'crowding-out effect' in fiscal policy refers to:

options.option_text: Government spending attracting more private investment

subject: Economics
explanation: When the government borrows heavily to finance deficit, it competes with private borrowers in the credit market, pushing up interest rates and reducing private investment — the 'crowding-out effect'.

stem: Capital expenditure in the Union Budget refers to expenditure that:

options.option_text: Is spent on salaries and subsidies
Is met from revenue receipts only
Creates assets or reduces liabilities (e.g., infrastructure, loan repayment)

subject: Economics
explanation: Capital expenditure creates assets (roads, dams, defence equipment) or reduces liabilities (loan repayment). Unlike revenue expenditure, it changes the government's asset-liability position.

stem: Automatic stabilisers in fiscal policy are mechanisms that:

options.option_text: Require a parliamentary vote each year
Automatically cushion the economy without discretionary action (e.g., unemployment benefits)

subject: Economics
explanation: Automatic stabilisers (like unemployment insurance, progressive taxes) expand or contract automatically with the business cycle, stabilising demand without requiring new legislation.

stem: The concept of 'zero-based budgeting' (ZBB) means:

options.option_text: Every budget item must be justified anew each period — no carryover from last year

subject: Economics
explanation: Under ZBB every expense must be re-justified each budget cycle from scratch, unlike incremental budgeting which adds a percentage to the prior year's base.

stem: Which of these is a capital receipt for the government?
subject: Economics
explanation: Borrowings are capital receipts (they create a liability). Income tax, dividends, and GST are revenue receipts.

stem: The Finance Commission of India is constituted every:
subject: Economics
explanation: Under Article 280, the Finance Commission is constituted every five years to recommend the distribution of tax revenues between the Centre and States.

stem: Fiscal consolidation refers to:

options.option_text: Reducing the fiscal deficit by cutting spending or raising revenues

subject: Economics
explanation: Fiscal consolidation means reducing the fiscal deficit through a mix of expenditure cuts and revenue enhancement, leading to a more sustainable public finance position.

stem: Which of the following increases fiscal deficit?

options.option_text: Defence capital expenditure not covered by receipts

subject: Economics
explanation: Capital expenditure on defence (or any expense) that exceeds total receipts (excluding borrowings) increases fiscal deficit. Higher tax collection and privatisation reduce the deficit.

stem: Stagflation poses a dilemma for fiscal policy because:

options.option_text: It requires both contractionary and expansionary policies simultaneously
The Finance Commission blocks countercyclical policy
Both recession and inflation co-exist, so stimulating demand worsens inflation while fighting inflation worsens unemployment

subject: Economics
explanation: Stagflation = stagnation (high unemployment) + inflation. Expansionary fiscal policy (to reduce unemployment) worsens inflation; contractionary policy (to curb inflation) worsens unemployment — the classic policy dilemma.
